title: Paper 1: guided textual analysis
summary: How Paper 1 works at SL and HL, what the four criteria reward, and a method for planning and writing a focused analysis of an unseen non-literary text.

keyterms.definition: Guided analysis of unseen non-literary texts: SL write on one of two (1 h 15 min), HL write on both (2 h 15 min).
The question printed with each Paper 1 text that suggests a focus; answering it is optional but helpful.
A text you have not studied before, analysed under exam conditions.
Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the text and well-supported interpretation (5 marks).
Analysis and evaluation: how well you analyse and evaluate the writer's choices and their effects (5 marks).
Focus and organization: a coherent, balanced and focused response (5 marks).
Language: clear, accurate, varied language with an appropriate register (5 marks).
Notes made on a text during reading to mark features, patterns and ideas.
A short quotation woven into your own sentence rather than dropped in on its own.
Naming devices without explaining their effect; a common weakness that limits marks.

questions.prompt: At SL, what does Paper 1 require?
options: Analysis of one of two unseen non-literary passages in 1 h 15 min
Analysis of both passages in 2 h 15 min
A comparative essay on two literary works
Multiple-choice questions
questions.explanation: SL students choose one of two non-literary passages; HL students write on both.

questions.statement: At HL, Paper 1 is worth 40 marks because candidates write two analyses of 20 marks each.
questions.explanation: HL candidates analyse both passages, each marked out of 20 using the same criteria.

questions.text: Each Paper 1 text comes with a ___ question that suggests a possible focus.
questions.explanation: Using the guiding question is optional, but it offers a ready-made way into the text.

questions.prompt: Match the Paper 1 criterion to what it rewards.
questions.explanation: Each criterion is worth 5 marks, giving 20 marks per analysis.

questions.prompt: Which criterion is most affected by a response that describes what the text says without explaining how its features work?
options: A only
B: analysis and evaluation
D: language
None
questions.explanation: Analysis and evaluation reward explaining how choices create meaning and judging their effectiveness.

questions.statement: Paper 1 texts can include visual elements such as images, layout and typography, which you are expected to analyse.
questions.explanation: Non-literary texts like adverts, infographics and web pages often rely on visual features.

questions.prompt: What is the weighting of Paper 1 at both SL and HL?
questions.explanation: Paper 1 counts for 35% at both levels.

questions.text: Naming devices without explaining their effect is called technique ___.
questions.explanation: Always link a device to its effect on the audience and the writer's purpose.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows the best language for criterion D?
options: The writer uses lots of good words to make it good.
The writer's clipped, imperative sentences create an urgent, almost military tone.
Its like really persuasive and stuff.
Words are used.
questions.explanation: Precise, varied vocabulary and accurate grammar in a formal register score highly.

questions.statement: Paper 1 passages are taken from the literary works you studied in class.
questions.explanation: Paper 1 uses unseen non-literary texts; studied literary works are for Paper 2.

questions.prompt: Order an effective SL Paper 1 process.
items: Read both texts and choose one
Annotate for audience, purpose and key features
Write a thesis and plan paragraphs
questions.explanation: Roughly 15–20 minutes of reading and planning usually pays off in focus and organization.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest Paper 1 introduction sentence?
options: This text is about a gym.
In this advert, the gym persuades young professionals that fitness is a route to status, using aspirational imagery and clipped, commanding slogans.
I will analyse this text.
There are many techniques in this text.
questions.explanation: It identifies text type, audience, purpose and methods: a clear thesis.

questions.text: A short quotation woven smoothly into your own sentence is an ___ quotation.
questions.explanation: Embedded quotations keep analysis fluent and precise.

questions.prompt: What is usually the best way to organise body paragraphs?
options: By ideas or effects, each linked to the thesis
Line by line, summarising each sentence
One paragraph per device, in alphabetical order
By word count
questions.explanation: Organising by effects or ideas avoids narration and supports a coherent argument.

questions.statement: Going through a text line by line from beginning to end is the only acceptable structure.
questions.explanation: A linear approach can work if it stays analytical, but it risks summary. Thematic structures often score better for focus.

questions.prompt: Match the weak habit to a better alternative.
questions.explanation: These swaps shift a response from description to analysis.

options: Judging how effectively the writer's choices achieve their purpose
Saying whether you agree with the topic
Giving the text a score out of 10
Correcting the writer's grammar
questions.explanation: Evaluation weighs effectiveness, e.g. noting that a statistic is persuasive but its source is vague.

questions.text: Marking features and ideas on the text as you read is called ___.
questions.explanation: Annotate with purpose: look for patterns, shifts and links to the guiding question.

questions.prompt: You have 10 minutes left and no conclusion. What is the best move?
options: Write a brief conclusion that returns to your thesis and synthesises your points
Start a new body paragraph on a minor detail
Write nothing more
Rewrite your introduction
questions.explanation: A short synthesising conclusion supports focus and organization.

questions.prompt: Which is a good way to use the guiding question?
options: Ignore the text and answer the question generally
Use it to shape your thesis while still exploring other significant features
Copy it as your first sentence and stop
Answer it in one word
questions.explanation: The guiding question is a starting point; strong responses go beyond it while staying focused.
